usage: Said when someone freezes up or gets caught off guard.
I was so caught off guard
-잖아 invites shared understanding: 'you know I was flustered, right?'
examples: 갑자기 영어로 물어봐서 완전 당황했어.
They suddenly asked me in English so I totally froze.
Very relatable for a foreigner-in-Korea scenario, reversed — being put on the spot.
카드가 안 돼서 계산대에서 당황했어.
My card got declined and I panicked at the checkout.
계산대 = the cashier/checkout counter; everyday convenience-store/cafe vocab.
당황하면 한국어가 하나도 안 나와.
When I get flustered, no Korean comes out at all.
안 나오다 here = 'doesn't come out (of my mouth)', natural for forgetting words.
nuance: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard (not long-term panic). It's the perfect word for those 'my brain went blank' moments. 당황스럽다 (adjective) describes a situation as 'awkward/bewildering'. The passive-ish 당황하다 already covers the felt experience, so 당황돼 is non-standard — use 당황했어.
mistakes: Saying 당황돼 — unlike 걱정/긴장, 당황하다 is not commonly used with 되다; stick to 당황해 / 당황했어.

usage: Teasing a partner or friend; playful tone is common.
For envy-without-resentment ('lucky you!'), Koreans say 부럽다, NOT 질투하다.
examples: 남친이 여사친 많아서 좀 질투해.
My boyfriend has a lot of female friends so I get a bit jealous.
남친 = boyfriend (남자친구), 여사친 = female friend (여자 사람 친구) — essential dating slang.
친구가 나보다 잘돼서 질투하는 내가 너무 싫어.
I hate that I'm jealous of my friend doing better than me.
잘되다 = 'to go well / succeed'; honest self-talk, very natural.
걔 인스타 보면 가끔 질투 나.
When I see their Instagram I sometimes get jealous.
질투(가) 나다 = 'jealousy arises' is more natural than 질투하다 for a passing feeling; 걔 = 'that person'.
nuance: Crucial distinction: 부럽다 = harmless envy ('lucky you, I wish I had that') and is what you say 90% of the time. 질투하다 / 질투 나다 implies a sharper, often romantic or competitive jealousy. Telling someone 부러워 is friendly; accusing them of 질투해 can sting. For the felt state, 질투(가) 나 ('I feel jealous') sounds more natural than 질투해.
mistakes: Using 질투하다 where English 'jealous' just means envious — say 부럽다 instead, e.g. 'You went to Jeju? 부럽다!' not 질투해.

usage: The standard motivational line — friends, coaches, dramas all use it.
-(으)ㄹ래 expresses your own decision/intention; resigned tone.
examples: 다이어트는 진작에 포기했어.
I gave up on the diet ages ago.
진작에 = 'long ago / already'; 다이어트 포기 is a relatable running joke.
집값 보고 서울에 집 사는 건 포기했어.
After seeing the prices, I gave up on buying a place in Seoul.
집값 = housing prices; a very real 20-30s concern. ~는 건 포기하다 = give up on -ing.
여기까지 왔는데 지금 포기하기엔 너무 아까워.
We've come this far — it'd be a waste to give up now.
아깝다 = 'too good to waste / regrettable'; ~기엔 = 'to (do something) is too...'
nuance: 포기하다 = to give up / abandon (a goal, plan, person). It pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or 는 거 (사는 건 포기하다). The famous self-deprecating slang 포기 (as in N포세대 — the 'give-up generation' that has given up on dating, marriage, kids, etc.) shows how loaded the word is for young Koreans facing economic pressure. 포기하지 마 is endlessly common encouragement.
mistakes: Spacing the negative wrong — it's 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), not 안 포기해.

usage: Encouraging someone to try something new/bold; 한번 = 'just once, give it a go'.
I love taking on new things
도전하다 takes 에 for the target of the challenge.
examples: 올해는 마라톤에 도전해 보려고.
This year I'm going to try taking on a marathon.
~에 도전하다; ~(으)려고 = 'I intend/plan to'. Common New Year goal talk.
새로운 분야에 도전하고 싶어서 이직했어.
I changed jobs because I wanted to take on a new field.
이직하다 = 'to change jobs', big in 20-30s career talk; 분야 = field/area.
매운 거 잘 못 먹는데 불닭 한번 도전해 볼게.
I'm bad with spicy food but I'll give fire-noodles a try.
불닭 = 불닭볶음면, the famous super-spicy instant noodle; 도전해 볼게 = 'I'll give it a try'.
nuance: 도전하다 = to challenge oneself / take on (a goal, a new experience). It's overwhelmingly positive and aspirational — think job changes, new hobbies, trying scary food. It takes 에 (목표에 도전하다, 시험에 도전하다). Note: it does NOT mean 'to challenge a person to a fight/argument' — that's 도전장을 내밀다 or just context. 도전해 봐 ('give it a try') is everyday encouragement.
mistakes: Using 을/를 instead of 에 — it's 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), not 마라톤을 도전하다.

usage: Sincere promise to put in effort; softer and warmer than a firm guarantee.
-는 중이야 = 'in the middle of'; common honest reply.
examples: 한국어 늘려고 매일 노력하고 있어.
I'm making an effort every day to improve my Korean.
늘다 ('to improve/increase'); ~(으)려고 expresses purpose. Perfect learner sentence.
노력한 만큼 결과가 안 나와서 속상해.
The results don't match my effort, and it's upsetting.
~한 만큼 = 'as much as (I) did'; 속상하다 = 'to be upset/heartsick'.
관계는 한 사람만 노력하면 안 돼.
A relationship can't work if only one person tries.
Relatable dating wisdom; 관계 = relationship, ~만 ...면 안 돼 = 'it won't do if only...'.
nuance: 노력하다 = to make an effort, try hard, put in work toward a goal. It implies sustained, earnest effort (vs 도전하다's 'take on a new challenge', or a one-time 한번 해 보다 'give it a try'). 노력할게 ('I'll try') is a very common, sincere thing to say. Pairs with ~(으)려고 노력하다 = 'try to (do)'. Highly valued culturally — effort itself is praised.
mistakes: Confusing with 도전하다: 노력하다 = sustained effort, 도전하다 = taking on a fresh challenge. 'I'll try harder' is 더 노력할게, not 더 도전할게.

usage: Just hold on a little longer
Gritty encouragement — survive the hard part.
I have to hold out till payday
Very real 20s money humor; 월급날 = payday.
examples: 커피로 버티면서 시험 기간 넘겼어.
I got through exam season running on coffee.
~(으)로 버티다 = 'get by on'; 시험 기간 = exam period. Universal student life.
상사가 진상이라 1년 버티고 퇴사했어.
My boss was awful so I held out a year and then quit.
진상 = a nasty/awful person (slang); 퇴사하다 = 'to quit one's job'.
여기서 포기하지 말고 끝까지 버텨 보자.
Don't give up here — let's tough it out to the end.
끝까지 = 'to the very end'; pairs naturally with 포기하지 말다.
nuance: 버티다 = to hold out, hang on, endure/survive a hard stretch — often financially or against pressure (a tough job, no money, exam season). It's grittier and more 'street' than 견디다, and is the go-to word for young Koreans joking about surviving until payday or sticking it out at a bad job. Regular ㅣ-stem: 버티 + 어 → 버텨; past 버텼어.
mistakes: Writing the past as 버티었어 or 버텼써 — the correct form is 버텼어 (버티 + 었어 contracted).

usage: ~아/어 줘서 고마워 = 'thanks for (doing) for me'; very common.
위로가 되다 = 'to be a comfort'; natural reply when someone's words helped.
examples: 친구가 힘들 때 옆에서 위로해 줬어.
My friend comforted me when I was going through a hard time.
옆에서 ('by my side') + 위로해 주다 ('comfort me') — the giving form 주다 is almost always attached.
말없이 안아주는 게 제일 큰 위로였어.
Just being hugged without words was the biggest comfort.
위로 as a noun ('comfort'); 말없이 = 'without words', 안아주다 = 'to hug (someone)'.
오늘 같은 날엔 치맥이 최고의 위로지.
On a day like today, chicken and beer is the best comfort.
치맥 = 치킨+맥주 (fried chicken + beer), the iconic Korean comfort combo; ~지 = knowing agreement.
nuance: 위로하다 = to comfort/console someone going through pain or loss. In practice it almost always appears as 위로해 주다 (comfort someone — with the benefactive 주다) or as the noun 위로 (위로가 되다 'to be a comfort', 위로를 받다 'to be comforted'). It's warm and a bit emotionally weighty — for everyday cheering-up you might lean on 응원하다 instead. 치맥 as 위로 is peak Korean culture.
mistakes: Dropping the benefactive 주다 — 'I comforted my friend' is 친구를 위로해 줬어, not just 친구를 위로했어 (which sounds clinical/detached).

usage: I'll always be rooting for you
Warm, supportive send-off; common in messages and goodbyes.
Cheer me on / Wish me luck
Asking for support before a big thing; ~아/어 줘 = 'do it for me'.
examples: 새 직장 잘되길 응원할게!
I'm rooting for your new job to go well!
잘되길 (= 잘되기를) 응원하다 = 'cheer for it to go well'; sweet, everyday support.
나 항상 네 편이고 응원해.
I'm always on your side and rooting for you.
네 편이다 = 'to be on your side'; pairs naturally with 응원하다.
손흥민 경기 있어서 친구들이랑 모여서 응원했어.
There was a Son Heung-min match so we gathered to cheer.
응원하다 also = cheering for a sports team; 모이다 = 'to gather'. Football-watch culture.
nuance: 응원하다 = to cheer on / root for / support — both literally (a sports team) and emotionally (a friend's goals). For everyday encouragement, 응원해 / 응원할게 is lighter and more upbeat than 위로하다 (which is for someone in pain). Telling someone 응원할게 is one of the warmest, most natural things to say. Often takes the benefactive 응원해 줘 when asking for support.
mistakes: Confusing 응원하다 (cheer on / support toward a goal) with 위로하다 (comfort in sadness) — you 응원해 someone facing a challenge, but 위로해 someone who's hurting.
